question.text: The Vindhya Event-Driven Fund (Cat III AIF) has a corpus of INR 200 crore across 20,00,000 units, giving a gross NAV of Rs. 1,000. An illiquid position (INR 20 crore book value) is identified as stressed and is SIDE-POCKETED. After side-pocketing, what is the main-scheme NAV and the side-pocket NAV per unit?

answer.text: Main NAV Rs. 1,000; side-pocket NAV Rs. 0 (written off)
Main NAV Rs. 900; side-pocket NAV Rs. 100 per unit (each unitholder's proportional share of the INR 20 cr segregated at its last marked value)
Main NAV Rs. 800; side-pocket NAV Rs. 200
Main NAV Rs. 1,000; side-pocket NAV Rs. 1,000 (duplicate units)

explanation.text: The Logic: Side-pocketing isolates an illiquid asset into a separate sub-scheme at its last marked value. Here, INR 20 cr (illiquid) / 20,00,000 units = Rs. 100 per unit is segregated in the side-pocket. The remaining INR 180 cr / 20,00,000 units = Rs. 900 per unit is the main-scheme NAV. Each existing unitholder retains 1 main unit (Rs. 900) plus 1 side-pocket unit (Rs. 100) per original unit, so total economic exposure is preserved while the main NAV becomes free of the stressed asset's mark uncertainty. The Trap: Option A wrongly writes the asset down to zero at segregation — side-pocketing preserves last marked value, it does not impair. Option C miscalculates the corpus split. Option D doubles unit count without an economic basis. Note: Side-pocket NAV splitting, the post-segregation subscription treatment, and the segregation mechanics described above are not explicitly set out in the cited XIX-E (Category III AIF Managers) workbook pages, which support class/series NAV allocation concepts generally. The framing reflects general industry/regulatory practice for handling illiquid assets in pooled funds.
